articles.title: Mongolia President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa To Resign After $25 Million Bribery Allegations Over Railway Project
articles.description: Reported by: Karl Sexton | Timothy Jones AP, AFP Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa said Tuesday that he would resign after the opposition Democratic Party accused him of profiting from a government railway project. At a press conference, Khurelsukh said he was being "falsely accused and defamed" but would resign in order to "restore my good name." He has pledged to cooperate with investigators. Before the resignation takes effect, it must first be accepted by parliament, the State Great Khural. What are the accusations against Khurelsukh? Nyambaatar Khishgee, the ex-mayor of Ulaanbaatar, the country's capital, on Saturday accused Khurelsukh of receiving $25 million (around €23 million) linked to the Tavantolgoi-Gashuunsukhait railway project. The railway connects the Tavantolgoi coal mine with the Mongolian port of Gashuunsukhait on the Chinese border, a central hub for the export of coal from Mongolia to China. The former mayor belongs to the president's party, but is part of a different faction within it. The opposition Democratic Party picked up on the accusations and called on Khurelsukh to step down. According to the allegations, Khurelsukh received the money in bribes from the conglomerate Bodi International LLC, which received the contract to construct the railway without a competitive tender. Bodi on Monday denied having paid any cash bribes to obtain the contract. Infighting in Khurelsukh's party Khurelsukh, from the Mongolian People's Party, has been president since 2021. But infighting has caused disruption in the party in recent years, with three prime ministers taking office in just nine months. Khurelsukh paid a state visit to Germany from October 19 to 22 this year. (Disclaimer: This report first appeared on Deutsche Welle, and has been republished on ABP Live as part of a special arrangement. Apart from the headline, no changes have been made in the report by ABP Live.)

articles.title: Himachal Pradesh Holds Vendor Development Programme To Link MSMEs With Large Industries
articles.description: Himachal Pradesh Holds Vendor Development Programme To Link MSMEs With Large Industries Shimla, Nov 17 (KNN) A Vendor Development Programme (VDP) was organised at the Himachal Chamber of Commerce and Industry (HCCI), Paonta Sahib, under the Raising and Accelerating MSME Performance (RAMP) Scheme to strengthen business linkages between large industries and Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs). The programme was organised with the support of the Union Ministry of MSME and the Himachal Pradesh Department of Industries, in collaboration with Tinge Consultancy Pvt. Ltd. and Wonder Worx. Focus on Procurement and Market Access Representatives from the pharmaceutical, packaging, food processing and engineering sectors were briefed on procurement procedures, quality standards, technology upgradation, supply-chain integration, credit facilities and government support schemes. The sessions also covered vendor registration with large corporations, tendering procedures, documentation requirements, the Government e-Marketplace (GeM) portal and market linkages. A buyer-seller interaction session involving Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs) and Original Product Manufacturers (OPMs) provided entrepreneurs an opportunity to explore business partnerships and connect with large industrial buyers. Vendors also showcased their products at an exhibition. Experts encouraged MSMEs to improve product quality, upgrade technology and strengthen their business capabilities to become part of the supply chains of larger industries. (KNN Bureau)

articles.title: Sumanta Chaudhuri: MSME Utilisation Is Critical to the Success of India's Free Trade Agreements [Retired IAS Officer, International Trade Specialist, India]
articles.description: Sumanta Chaudhuri Interview Retired IAS officer, international trade policy expert, and former CII Principal Advisor Sumanta Chaudhuri reflects on decades of public administration, multilateral trade negotiations, and agricultural reform. He discusses aligning trade policy with MSME growth, balancing energy security with coal transition, and the leadership lessons learned across key government ministries. Q. Could you take us through your professional journey, from joining the Indian Administrative Service in 1985 to working on international trade policy and recommending businesses today? My professional journey began when I joined the Indian Administrative Service in 1985. Over the years, I had the opportunity to work across several key areas of public policy, including international trade and investment, industrial development, public sector enterprises, energy, and welfare of small and marginal farmers including agricultural marketing. A significant part of my career was spent in the Ministry of Commerce, Government of India, where I worked on multilateral trade negotiations at the World Trade Organisation and served as India's Counsellor at its Permanent Mission in Geneva. I also had the privilege of serving as India's Chief Negotiator for several free trade agreements, including those with ASEAN, Malaysia, and Thailand as well as RCEP. Later, as Secretary in the Ministry of Coal, I worked on policy strategy for upgrading and modernising coal production and distribution and for operationalization of auctioned coal mines, while my role at the Small Farmers' Agri-Business Consortium involved promoting electronic agricultural markets and supporting Farmer Producer Organisations in their entire lifecycle. After retiring from the IAS in January 2021, I continued contributing to international trade policy as Principal Advisor, International Trade Policy at the Confederation of Indian Industry. I have also worked as an Independent Director, taught Trade laws and public policy at leading institutions, and have been taking part in several international forums. Looking back, my journey has been about understanding and analysing complex policy challenges, negotiating practical solutions, and using that experience to contribute to India's economic development. Q. You have worked at the intersection of governance, economics, and international relations. How do you ensure that policies are not only successful on paper but effectively implemented? What pitfalls should one try to avoid? Every policy has two equally crucial aspects, design and implementation, which need to be complementary and synchronised. Design requires choosing between alternatives based to the extent possible on identifiable criteria followed by a broad cost-benefit analysis. For public policies affecting a considerable number of stakeholders, it is important to look at relevant externalities and the broader ecosystem while undertaking the pros and cons as well as impacts on other policies. For example, we were exploring various alternatives for developing quality industrial infrastructure in West Bengal. Initially, we had to find and analyse alternative models like Industrial parks owned, operated and leased by Government to entrepreneurs; Public-Private Partnerships (PPP); outsourcing to PMUs. In parallel, factor in the land availability and relevant land laws including on acquisition, direct purchase from the landowners or contract-based models; labour laws; nature of industry likely to be attracted and pricing/ financing options. After a lot of deliberation and iterations, we were able to narrow down to a couple of feasible choices. For this, it is advisable to undertake wide consultations with all the concerned stakeholders. On occasions, there are misunderstandings/apprehensions amongst some of them or worse, deliberate attempts to muddy the waters. Explaining the rationale and benefits is critical and the ability to adapt and change if the discussions bring out parameters or perspectives that the policy makers may have missed out. At the same time, this should not be mistaken as license to disrupt or stall and there maybe situations when toughness and resolve need to be demonstrated for larger public good. The extent to which your stakeholder consultations during the formulation stage are broadly able to satisfy different cross-sections and create a sense of belonging or familiarity for at least the key ones determine the acceptability, effectiveness, and pace of the implementation. It is possible that on occasions, "good" policies get stuck at implementation stage either due to some design deficiencies, or vested interests trying to torpedo the success or simply because the implementation machinery has no buy-in or incentive to deliver. While the first reason has been covered previously, for the other bottlenecks, it is always necessary to have well analysed back-up plans in case the first line of delivery gets stuck. At this stage too, it is imperative to do a proper awareness and handholding campaign with all stakeholders and remove misconceptions, which are likely. Also, one needs to be flexible as permissible under the policy and not completely rigid on the way forward. In the earlier example, there were vested interests who believed their stranglehold would be diluted. Post policy formulation, extensive awareness creation through industry chambers, display on relevant websites, public advertisements and a system of continuous feedback and online monitoring were used to streamline the policy and plug loopholes. Q. As India negotiates free trade agreements with major economies, how can the country ensure that small businesses and local industries benefit alongside large corporations? This is an extremely pertinent issue as Indian MSMEs contribute to our exports. Utilisation of numerous FTAs that India has entered recently can only succeed if the MSMEs are on board and newer entrants are both motivated and assisted in doing so. The first stage of this mission is to create proper understanding on the challenges and opportunities arising from each of these FTAs, remove many doubts amongst them and provide them with requisite tools to navigate these FTAs. For this purpose, toolkits have been devised by International Trade Policy Division at Confederation of Indian industry (CII) which I had the opportunity to lead. MSME Manual has been developed as well as a Standards Portal named TESIP which is a unique one-stop shop for all relevant information relating to both product and sustainability standards for major commodity groups and the prevalent ecosystem in India on Testing Labs; Conformity assessment bodies and standard setting bodies. Secondly, it is valuable to obtain feedback from small businesses who try to avail of the FTA benefits regarding procedural hurdles, interpretation of provisions of the agreement or lack of implementation of features which would become operational post entry into force of the agreements in both partners' jurisdictions, including customs procedures; rules of origin documentation/certification; adherence to standards/ technical regulations and testing facilities; appropriate work permits for relevant categories of natural persons desirous of providing services in the other jurisdiction and other regulatory barriers that impinge on the market access provided. Third, locating and disseminating Success Stories of MSMEs and bigger players navigating the FTA universe, could play a pivotal role in motivating fellow exporters/ services suppliers, nothing succeeds like success! Q. You have witnessed India's trade negotiations at the WTO and its evolving global role. What has changed most significantly in how India approaches international trade? While India was a founder member of both the WTO and its predecessor, GATT, it was a minor and at times reluctant participant till the Uruguay Round launch of WTO in 1995. It was around the time that WTO was taking birth that India began its liberalisation journey with the Reform process initiated in 1991 which included removing many of the fetters on international trade and later bringing domestic Indian laws in consonance with WTO provisions, including the TRIPS agreement. A major change came around the Doha Ministerial Conference of the WTO in 2001 where two big ticket items were on the agenda. The negotiations and the outcomes changed both our approach as well as the perspective of trade partners on India's WTO journey. India was at the forefront of the contentious debate regarding TRIPS and Public Health in the backdrop of the AIDS epidemic devastating particularly Africa and other developing countries with AIDS medicines' patents obtained by the multinational drug companies putting the drugs outside the reach of most patients. This led to the Declaration on TRIPS & Public Health at Doha providing a much-needed balance between patent rights and right to Public Health for all citizens especially in the case of epidemics. Second, was the spirited fight by developing countries spearheaded by India on preventing the inclusion of the so called "Singapore issues" being forced on all WTO members by EU, US, and other developed countries. At the end, India stood alone to block such a forcible inclusion, clearly against wishes of the vast majority of developing countries which ultimately resulted in three of these controversial issues, namely, Investment, Competition Policy and Transparency in Government Procurement being abandoned from the WTO agenda. India succeeded in reversing the earlier narrative under GATT and WTO of US & EU virtually dictating the AGENDA. Post 2001, the voice of developing countries and their effective participation in WTO agenda setting and rule-making was transformed to a certain extent. A third example of the proactive participation of India subsequently was in the Services negotiations under the Doha Round where India was credited as being one of the principal architects of the Services Text adopted at the Hong Kong Ministerial Conference of the WTO in 2005 better known as "Annex C". I had the crucial role of piloting the Services negotiations for India both as a capital-based delegate and from the Geneva Mission and it is a matter of satisfaction that India could shape the modalities on Services negotiations in WTO. Unfortunately, The Doha Round fell apart and was abandoned for a variety of reasons and at the same time, the emergence of China which joined the WTO in 2001 changed fundamentally the trade power equations with China successfully taking over the mantle in manufacturing and exports. US interest in WTO started waning, achieving consensus amongst the large and varied WTO membership was proving futile and a spate of newer, so called "non-trade" issues emerged. Alternative channels started being explored both within and outside the WTO. Newer alliances were formed and plurilateral outcomes were increasingly being sought to overcome the consensus principle which India opposed on systemic grounds. Simultaneously, efforts continued to incorporate newly emerging issues relating to climate change mitigation, E-commerce/ Digital Trade, and Investment facilitation both multilaterally and through plurilateral initiatives. Consequently, India is facing such new challenges in WTO which it must cleverly navigate and engage in, protecting its own national interests while accommodating other WTO members' viewpoints. India is at a crossroad in terms of how it envisages the future role of the WTO and its own approach. Q. While leading initiatives such as e-NAM, you worked to connect farmers with digital markets. What are the biggest barriers preventing small farmers from receiving better prices for their produce? Small and marginal farmers who are the predominant category in the agricultural landholding pyramid face myriad challenges in obtaining competitive prices for their produce. The principal barrier is the complete lack of countervailing power for such individual farmers which forces them to be only price takers, not price makers for all aspects—whether prices of inputs or produce prices. Consolidation of landholdings is not possible, so the only practical route is aggregation of farmers into larger groups which is the main aim of promoting Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs). FPOs can partially overturn this bargaining power deficit provided they become effective, efficient interlocutors for the farmers in all their interactions with external agents for inputs, quality control, warehousing, marketing, and value addition/processing. For this, FPOs must be nurtured, handheld and assisted over their lifecycle till they become self-sufficient and large enough in terms of economies of scale and bargaining power. I was fortunate to be part of this transformative journey. The second challenge facing the small farmers are post harvesting issues relating to storage, scientific quality assessment of produce, minimising crop damage, alternative price discovery mechanisms, financing, and value addition/processing of raw produce. The E-NAM project for online digital price discovery through live auctions instead of the earlier dependence on Arhatiyas for buying their produce and managing other needs like finance was one of the principal instruments to overcome these deficiencies along with the FPO movement. Bringing bulk buyers of agricultural produce like processors, exporters, retail chains etc directly in contact with the FPOs is an essential ingredient which could be a win-win situation for all. The FPO collection centres or the farm gate collection must be the epicentre for all such activities with instruments for assaying, warehousing facilities inhouse or through negotiable warehousing receipts which could also serve as collateral for loans. Identifying local skilled workforce to manage the FPOs professionally as a profit-making entity; training and awareness of the office bearers as well as all producers is also critical. Business development of FPOs spanning seed and fertiliser dealerships, tie-ups with large institutional buyers who handhold quality and promote best crop practices is a vital cog. Such a desired policy framework was put together largely by agencies like SFAC where I was MD, NAFED, NABARD and others but unfortunately this has not borne the expected fruits for a host of reasons. Hopefully, this will change as this seems to be the "equilibrium solution" for a highly vexatious and multi-dimensional problem. Q. As India balances economic growth with climate commitments, how should policymakers approach the transition from coal to cleaner energy without compromising livelihoods and energy security? The concept of "Fair Transition" which is now accepted globally as the SOP for energy transition from carbon intensive energy sources to climate neutral renewable sources is a huge challenge in India given our fairly large dependence on coal despite the wonderful strides India has made in renewables particularly Solar energy and the considerable work force that is dependent on the coal ecosystem. The strategy must contain several components: i) The most crucial and the most difficult is to ensure that entire communities who have survived only on coal mining and ancillary activities for a couple of generations are provided alternative livelihoods and revenue streams. Here, employment-based apprenticeship and training is necessary. Both the public sector coal companies and private firms must use not only their CSR for these purposes but ensure early tie-ups with local industry and ITIs to match their skilling with market needs. This can also be dovetailed with self-employment / entrepreneurial schemes at the district level. A handful of districts accounts for a lion's share of the coal mining and alternative, holistic Plans need to be formulated for human capital development and related infrastructure. ii) Production and distribution of coal needs to be made more environmentally friendly through appropriate use of technology including Coal Gasification which converts solid coal to Syn Gas and generates highly valuable by-products like ammonia, urea, methanol; coal washing to reduce ash content and sulphur that reduces carbon emissions; captive use of renewable energy for running the coal mines and use of modern mining equipment that is more carbon efficient. Similarly, transportation of coal can be made more carbon neutral by mandating First Mile connectivity which was introduced in the Ministry of Coal for projects exceeding a certain annual production target in 2019. This cuts down the road transport which reduces emissions, air pollution, prevents pilferage of coal and damage to roads by heavy vehicular traffic, instead conveyor belts transport coal from the mine to the railway sidings. This is now being practiced for all coal mines. iii) The Coal Mining Closure plan which is an integral part of the overall Mining plan involving scientific closure must positively involve the affected community and transform the abandoned coal pits into eco friendly zones/ waterbody restoration which is being successfully done. Thus, the lifecycle of a coal mine does not end with abandoning the coal mine but should restart with other productive uses. Q. Having spent decades in public service and later moved into advisory and academic roles, what is one belief about governance that your professional experience has fundamentally changed or assertively confirmed? When I joined the Civil Services, I frankly did not have much idea of how governance works or does not work, given also that I came from a family of academicians. However, one did have some idealistic notions that an individual alone can transform the system and bring change. From my own experiences and of others, I realised quickly that while individuals do make a difference, the desired reengineering / metamorphosis is contingent on team building and leading by example. It is imperative to earn the trust and respect of team members not just by virtue of hierarchy but through leadership, compassion, depth of knowledge and readiness to take even tough decisions based on available facts and opinions. Another common perception that one needs to "go after" the recalcitrant staff to reduce corruption and red-tapism was also reshaped by circumstances where system reengineering, use of digital means to cut manual interactions and involving the former proved far more effective and sustainable. It is a question of striking the right chord, continuously acknowledging in public the contribution made by each member and creating in the end, both a sense of belonging and a sense of satisfaction when the team can deliver. The other characteristic I learnt and valued was being open and accessible to your peers, team members and other stakeholders while being mindful that the openness is not misused by others. One final lesson, in the end what matters most is the compassion, recognition and trust you bestow on others. Q. What is one book, movie, or series you absolutely love and would recommend everyone experience at least once? This is not an easy answer as everybody has their own perspective and likings. But given my lack of exposure on Civil Services, I rewatched the episodes of the famous BBC serial—"Yes Minister" not just for the entertainment which I had experienced the first time, but equally how to manage the relationship with the executive and legislature in real-life situations and balance interests. While the context was quite separate, I have imbibed some core lessons from this serial. Several books left an impression on me during my long journey in international trade including—"The World is Flat" by Thomas Friedman, "Breakout Nations" by Ruchir Sharma and many others. And finally, one enjoyed "The Argumentative Indian" by Amartya Sen. Bio Sumanta Chaudhuri is a retired 1985-batch Indian Administrative Service (IAS) officer with extensive experience in public administration, international trade, and economic policy. During his distinguished career, he served in several key positions in the Government of India, including Secretary in the Ministry of Coal, Joint Secretary in the Department of Commerce, and Counsellor at India's Permanent Mission to the World Trade Organization (WTO) in Geneva. He played a significant role in India's multilateral trade negotiations and served as India's Chief Negotiator for several free trade agreements, including those with ASEAN, RCEP, Malaysia, and Thailand. Following his retirement in January 2021, Chaudhuri continued to contribute to international trade policy and institutional development. He served as Principal Advisor for International Trade Policy at the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII), worked as an Independent Director at Kanoria Chemicals Limited, and taught trade laws and public policy at leading academic institutions. He has also contributed to international forums, including the WTO, World Bank, and United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), bringing his expertise to discussions on global trade, sustainable development, and economic cooperation. linkedin Interviewed By Ritika Tawar
